sentences.text: Barinasuchus is an extinct genus of sebecid mesoeucrocodylian, a member of the family Sebecidae. The genus was established by Alfredo Paolillo and Omar Linares in 2007, with the type species designated as B. arveloi.

This animal was heterodont, possessing two distinct types of teeth that resembled those of theropod dinosaurs rather than the laterally compressed, serrated edges found in modern crocodilians. The teeth located in the premaxilla and front maxilla were longer and more conical, while those further back were shorter and thinner. This unique dentition made Barinasuchus a formidable predator.

Knowledge of the animal's full anatomy is limited because the holotype—the specimen the species is based on—consists only of an incomplete articulated frontal skull and lower jaw. This material was recovered from the upper part of the Parángula Formation in Barinas, Venezuela, but the specimen was largely destroyed during excavation, leaving only the anterior half of the skull and mandible.

Barinasuchus possesses the largest skull of any known sebecosuchian, with preserved dimensions reaching 70 cm in length and 40 cm in height. Based on these measurements and comparisons with more complete relatives, the total skull length is estimated to be between 95 and 110 cm. The total length of the animal is estimated at nearly 6 meters, making it the largest known sebecid.
It was among the last and largest sebecids, outlasting others like Dentaneosuchus, possibly due to isolation within a northern South American ecosystem dominated by non-mammalian predators.
The genus was formally described by Paolillo and Linares in 2007.

The holotype was discovered by road workers near Qedabra Socó, Venezuela, in 1973 while they were building a road to El Toro. It was recovered from the upper part of the Parángula Formation, dating to the lower middle Miocene.
Although a large sebecid skeleton was found, the excavation process largely destroyed the remains, leaving only a partial snout and mandible which were later relocated to an institution in Barinas.

Barinasuchus primarily inhabited lacustrine environments, including the Pebas Mega-Wetland and adjacent regions during the Miocene. The earliest known specimen comes from the mid-Eocene Divisadero Largo Formation, which was deposited in a shallow lacustrine environment.

Barinasuchus and other similarly sized sebecosuchians appear to have been apex predators. Its dentition, resembling that of theropod dinosaurs, made it a formidable predator capable of hunting in these aquatic and terrestrial settings.

Because the postcranial skeleton and much of the skull are unknown due to the destruction of the holotype, researchers Molnar and Mequita de Vasconcellos used anatomical proxies to estimate its size. They used the baurusuchid genus Stratiotosuchus as a reference for this size estimation.

A 2025 analysis by Bravo et al. recovered Barinasuchus as the sister taxon to a clade containing the Lumbrera form and Sebecus species. In cladograms, it is classified as a Sebecosuchian of the family Sebecidae, closely related to the genus Lorosuchus and forming the sister taxon to the genera Ayllusuchus and Bretesuchus, indicating it represents a fairly basal lineage within the family.

Barinasuchus lived in Argentina, Peru, and Venezuela from the middle Eocene to the Late Miocene, approximately 42 to 11.6 million years ago. Fossils have been found in the Middle Eocene Divisadero Largo Formation of Argentina (tentatively assigned), the Middle Miocene Ipururo Formation of Peru, and the Parangula Formation of Venezuela. The genus lived from the Lutetian to the Tortonian stages, between 42 and 11 million years ago.

Langstonia was contemporaneous with Barinasuchus and lived in South America. Later specimens of Barinasuchus lived up to the middle Miocene in a northern South American ecosystem dominated by non-mammalian predators.
It is debated whether the extinction of Barinasuchus resulted from the loss of the Pebas Mega-Wetland or the diversification of mammalian predators and phorusrhacid birds.
